content.value: Water moves toward the more concentrated solution — toward the side with more dissolved solute, which is the side with proportionally less water. Reasoning in terms of the solute alone reverses it, since the solute is what appears in the description while the water is what actually moves. The reliable phrasing is that water follows solute. Predicting a cell's fate then becomes mechanical: place it in salty water and it loses water and shrivels; place it in pure water and it takes water in and swells. Separately, transport is only active when it works against a concentration gradient and spends ATP. Diffusion and osmosis are passive, and so is facilitated diffusion, even though a protein is involved — the protein provides a route, not a push. An answer choice describing a downhill movement as requiring energy is testing that distinction.

entries.label: Natural selection: the mechanism, stated as conditions

content.value: Natural selection is not a vague notion of the fittest winning; it is a specific mechanism that follows necessarily whenever four conditions hold. First, individuals in a population vary. Second, some of that variation is heritable — passed to offspring. Third, more offspring are produced than the environment can support, so not all survive to reproduce. Fourth, survival and reproduction are not random with respect to the variation: some heritable traits make an individual likelier to reproduce in that environment. Given those four, the favoured trait tends to rise in frequency generation after generation — not as a rule about any single generation, where chance still intervenes, but as the direction the population is pushed for as long as the conditions hold. Two consequences of that framing are heavily tested. Selection acts on individuals, whose traits determine whether they reproduce, but the thing that evolves is the population, whose allele frequencies shift across generations — an individual organism never evolves. And fitness in this context means reproductive success in a particular environment, not strength, size, or health. A trait that is advantageous in one environment can be a liability in another, so there is no such thing as a universally superior organism.

entries.label: Where variation comes from, and how species form

content.value: Selection can only work on variation that already exists, so its source matters. Mutations are the ultimate origin of new alleles — random changes in DNA, occurring regardless of whether they would be useful, and most are neutral or harmful rather than beneficial. Sexual reproduction then shuffles existing alleles into new combinations through crossing over, independent assortment, and the random pairing of gametes. Neither source is directed toward need. Speciation — the formation of a new species — generally requires populations to stop interbreeding. The common route is geographic separation: a mountain range rises, a river shifts, a few individuals colonize an island, and the separated groups accumulate different mutations under different selective pressures and different chance events. Given enough divergence they can no longer produce fertile offspring together even if reunited, and at that point they are separate species. Evolution also proceeds without selection: genetic drift is random change in allele frequencies, and it is powerful in small populations, where chance alone can eliminate a perfectly good allele.

entries.label: The evidence, and how organisms are classified

content.value: Several independent lines of evidence converge on common ancestry, and their independence is the argument. The fossil record shows sequences of change over time and transitional forms. Comparative anatomy shows homologous structures — the same bone arrangement in a human arm, a whale flipper, and a bat wing, used for entirely different purposes, which is what inheritance from a shared ancestor predicts and what independent design would not. Vestigial structures are reduced remnants of features that were functional in ancestors. Embryology shows shared developmental patterns among related groups. Molecular biology is the most quantitative line: essentially all life uses the same genetic code, and the degree of DNA similarity between two species tracks how recently they shared an ancestor. Classification now aims to reflect that ancestry. The three domains are Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya, and the traditional hierarchy runs domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species — each level more inclusive than the one below. Two organisms in the same genus are more closely related than two merely in the same order.

entries.label: Energy flow through an ecosystem

content.value: Producers — mostly plants and algae — capture light energy and make their own food; that is what autotroph means, and it is the base of nearly every food chain. Consumers eat other organisms: herbivores eat producers, carnivores eat other consumers, omnivores do both. Decomposers, mainly bacteria and fungi, break down dead material and return its nutrients to the soil and water. A food chain is one path through this; a food web is the realistic picture, since most organisms eat and are eaten by several others. The quantitative rule is the one items lean on: only about ten percent of the energy at one trophic level is available to the next, with the rest spent on the organism's own living or lost as heat. That is why food chains are short — rarely more than four or five links — and why an energy pyramid narrows sharply upward. The deepest point here is a contrast: energy flows one way through an ecosystem and leaves it as heat, while matter cycles. Carbon, nitrogen, and water are used repeatedly and returned; the energy that moved them is not recovered, which is why sunlight must keep arriving.

entries.label: Populations, limiting factors, cycles, and succession

content.value: A population grows rapidly when resources are abundant, then slows as it approaches the carrying capacity — the number the environment can sustain indefinitely. What holds it there are limiting factors, which come in two kinds. Density-dependent factors bite harder as the population grows: competition for food, disease transmission, predation. Density-independent factors strike regardless of numbers: a drought, a hard freeze, a fire. Species interactions are worth naming precisely — competition harms both, predation benefits one at the other's expense, and symbiosis covers mutualism (both benefit), commensalism (one benefits, the other is unaffected), and parasitism (one benefits at the other's expense). Matter moves through biogeochemical cycles: the water cycle through evaporation, condensation and precipitation; the carbon cycle through photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition and combustion; the nitrogen cycle depending on bacteria to convert atmospheric nitrogen into usable forms. Ecosystems also change over time through succession — primary succession beginning on bare rock with pioneer species such as lichens that build the first soil, and secondary succession following a disturbance like a fire, which is faster because soil already exists.

entries.label: Scenario

content.value: A farmer begins spraying a new insecticide on a beetle that damages his crop. The first season it kills almost every beetle. Each season he sprays the same chemical at the same dose, and each season it works a little less well; by the sixth season it barely helps, and the beetle population is as large as ever. A neighbour concludes that the beetles 'got used to' the spray and built up resistance the way a person builds tolerance to a drug. The questions are: what actually happened across those six seasons, why the neighbour's explanation is wrong, and what the farmer should do differently.

entries.label: Step 1 — Establish the starting condition before the first spray

content.value: The whole explanation depends on a fact about season one, before any chemical was applied: the beetle population already varied. Among millions of beetles, a small number happened to carry an allele — perhaps for an enzyme that breaks the chemical down, or a slightly different nerve receptor the chemical binds poorly — that made them harder to kill. Those alleles arose from random mutation, at whatever rate mutations occur, long before this insecticide existed and without reference to it. In season one they conferred no particular benefit and may have carried a small cost. This step is the one candidates skip, and skipping it makes every later step impossible to get right: the variation was there first, and the spray did not create it.

entries.label: Step 2 — Identify what the spray actually does

content.value: The insecticide is a selective pressure. It does not modify beetles; it sorts them. Susceptible beetles die and leave no offspring, while the few resistant ones survive and reproduce. Notice that this satisfies natural selection's four conditions exactly: there is variation, the variation is heritable, far more beetles are produced than survive, and survival is decidedly not random with respect to the trait. Note too what the 'almost every beetle' of season one really means — not that the spray was fully effective, but that a small surviving remnant was left, and that remnant was not a random sample of the original population. It was enriched in exactly the allele that mattered.

entries.label: Step 3 — Follow the change across generations

content.value: Because the survivors are the parents of the next generation, resistance alleles make up a larger share of season two's population than season one's. Spraying again applies the same filter to that already-shifted population, and the share rises again. Beetles reproduce quickly and in large numbers, so six seasons is many generations, and the compounding is fast — this is why resistance problems appear in insects and bacteria in years while comparable change in large slow-breeding animals takes far longer. State the outcome in the correct units: what changed is the frequency of an allele in the population. No individual beetle became more resistant during its life, and the beetles alive in season six are not tougher versions of the season-one beetles — they are the descendants of a different subset of them.

entries.label: Step 4 — Name precisely what the neighbour got wrong

content.value: The neighbour's explanation reverses cause and effect: it has the environment producing the trait in response to need, rather than selecting among traits that already varied. Three specific claims are wrong. Exposure did not cause the mutations — mutations are random with respect to what would be useful. Individual beetles did not adapt during their lifetimes — an individual's genes do not change because of what it experiences, and populations evolve while individuals do not. And beetles did not become resistant by 'trying' or by need — natural selection has no goal and supplies nothing on demand. The drug-tolerance analogy is the source of the error: tolerance in a person is a physiological change within one individual, which is a genuinely different process from a change in the composition of a population, and borrowing the word 'resistance' across the two hides the difference.

entries.label: Step 5 — Draw the management implication, and check for side effects

content.value: If the mechanism is selection, the remedy follows from it: stop applying the same relentless filter. Rotating among chemicals with different modes of action means no single resistance allele is favoured season after season. Leaving part of the crop unsprayed as a refuge keeps susceptible beetles in the population to breed with resistant ones, diluting the allele instead of concentrating it. Combining chemical control with crop rotation, resistant plant varieties and natural predators — integrated pest management — reduces how much selective pressure any one method applies. And there is an ecological side effect worth anticipating: a broad-spectrum insecticide also kills the predators and parasitoids that were quietly suppressing pests other than the target, so a previously harmless insect can surge into a new problem. Judging an intervention by its intended target alone misses the food web it was sprayed into.

entries.label: Conclusion

content.value: Rare resistance alleles already present in the population were selected for by repeated spraying, rising in frequency generation after generation until most beetles carried them. The neighbour's account fails because it has individuals changing in response to need rather than a population's composition shifting through differential survival. The transferable method is to ask, in this order: what variation existed before the pressure arrived, what the pressure selects for, and which unit is actually changing — individual or population. That last question resolves the majority of evolution items on this test, because the wrong answer choices are almost always written in the language of individuals adapting.

entries.label: Mistake: describing individuals as adapting to what they need

content.value: The single most common error in this area is saying an organism developed a trait because it needed one — giraffes stretching for high leaves and passing on longer necks, a moth darkening itself to match soot. Individuals do not evolve; populations do, across generations, through changes in the frequency of alleles that already varied. The environment selects among existing variation, it does not generate the variation it would find useful. Watch for the vocabulary that smuggles this in: organisms 'trying to', species 'developing' a trait 'in order to', mutations occurring 'in response to' a pressure. Those phrasings mark the distractor almost every time. When an item asks for an explanation of how a population came to have a trait, the correct choice begins with variation already present and proceeds through differential survival and reproduction.

entries.label: Mistake: treating evolution as progress toward something better

content.value: Evolution has no goal, no ladder, and no direction toward complexity or perfection. Traits are advantageous only relative to a particular environment at a particular time, so a change in the environment can turn an advantage into a liability without anything about the organism changing. There is no such thing as a more evolved species: every lineage alive today has been evolving for exactly the same length of time, and a bacterium is not an early draft of anything. Two related slips follow from this. 'Survival of the fittest' does not mean the strongest or healthiest survive — fitness is reproductive success, and an organism that lives long without reproducing has a fitness of zero. And extinction is not a failure of effort; it is what happens when an environment changes faster than a population's existing variation can accommodate.

entries.label: Mistake: thinking energy cycles through an ecosystem the way matter does

content.value: Matter cycles and energy does not. Carbon, nitrogen and water atoms are used, released, and used again indefinitely, which is why a closed system can keep recycling them. Energy enters as sunlight, moves up the trophic levels, and leaves as heat that no organism can recapture — which is why an ecosystem needs a continuous supply and cannot run on what it already has. The arithmetic follows: roughly ten percent of the energy at one level reaches the next, so a producer level supporting a large biomass supports a much smaller one above it, and food chains run out after four or five links. Two conclusions items ask for directly: an energy pyramid is always widest at the producers, and a given area of land can feed far more people growing crops than raising livestock on them, because the livestock adds a trophic level and discards about ninety percent of the energy in doing so.

entries.label: Mistake: expecting a change in an ecosystem to have only its direct effect

content.value: Removing a predator does not simply mean more prey. The prey population can overshoot its carrying capacity, strip the vegetation it depends on, and then crash further than it would have under predation — while the plants it overgrazed, and everything depending on those plants, change too. Food webs transmit effects along paths that are not obvious from the organism named in the question, and items in this area usually reward the answer that traces two steps rather than one. Two related errors travel with this. Carrying capacity is not a hard ceiling a population politely stops at; populations routinely overshoot it and are then cut back, sometimes severely. And an introduced species is disruptive not because it is foreign but because it may arrive without the predators, parasites, and competitors that limited it at home — which is a statement about the web it entered, not about the organism itself.
